1hP3Ej8XXiEFVd7U1VFk6YH3YtsEI9UowIwQJqhs.title: The Captain Who Sank His Own Ship
lines: A German captain sank nine British cargo ships without killing a single person, and whenever he took a crew prisoner, he welcomed them and apologized for sinking their ship.

But when some British warships hit his ship about 70 times, he ended up limping into a port in Uruguay, where he was told he had only 72 hours to leave, while the British sent fake radio messages that a huge fleet with an aircraft carrier was waiting outside to seize his ship but since it carried Germany's secret new radar there was no way he would let them take it,
So instead of giving up his country’s secrets he detonated explosives he had planted on board, which tore the ship apart,
And since he couldn't bear anyone thinking he sank his ship to save his own life, three days later he shot himself .

entities.name: Hans Wilhelm Langsdorff
entities.look: A 45-year-old German naval captain (born 20 March 1894), with the rank of Kapitän zur See. He wears the midnight-blue Kriegsmarine officer's service uniform. Line officers wore gold sleeve rings beneath a gold five-pointed star; four rings are shown for Kapitän zur See. His peaked cap has a single row of gold oak leaves on the peak, which marks the staff-officer grades Korvettenkapitän to Kapitän zur See (admirals had a double row). A white summer jacket and a white cap cover existed, and he was photographed dressed in white aboard in 1939. He was wounded in the battle of 13 December. For his death on 20 December, sources say he wore full dress uniform and lay on the ship's battle ensign. The face and build should be copied from the real December 1939 photos below; no written source I found describes his height, hair or features.

facts.fact: Born 20 March 1894 in Bergen auf Rügen; Kapitän zur See; aged 45 at his death on 20 December 1939
Promoted to Captain on 1 January 1937; took command of Admiral Graf Spee in October 1938; Iron Cross 2nd Class at Jutland 1916
Graf Spee was hit about 70 times, with 36 killed and 60 wounded; Langsdorff was among the wounded
He shot himself in full dress uniform, lying on the ship's battle ensign
He died in his room at the Hotel de Inmigrantes in Buenos Aires (English Wikipedia says the 'Naval Hotel'; one Spanish report says the naval arsenal)
Kriegsmarine line officers wore sleeve stripes beneath a gold star; the officer service uniform was midnight blue; the white summer jacket had epaulettes but no sleeve stripes
Staff-officer (Korvettenkapitän to Kapitän zur See) peaked caps carry a single row of gold oak leaves on the visor
The blue cap was officially worn with a white cover from 20 April to 30 September; rank is shown by four sleeve rings for this grade group

photos.shows: Langsdorff on the Montevideo quay talking with the German envoy Langmann, December 1939
Langsdorff with German officials and crew at the Montevideo funeral of the Graf Spee battle dead, December 1939
Langsdorff aboard Admiral Graf Spee, 1939

entities.name: Admiral Graf Spee
entities.look: A Deutschland-class Panzerschiff ('pocket battleship'): 186 m long, 14,890 t design displacement. Main guns are six 28 cm guns in two triple turrets, one forward and one aft of the superstructure. Eight 15 cm guns sit in single mounts amidships, with three twin 10.5 cm AA mounts. There are two quadruple torpedo tubes on the stern. Forward is a tall enclosed tower superstructure (the foremast) topped by the main rangefinder. On top of that rangefinder sits the secret Seetakt radar's rectangular 'mattress' antenna. She has one funnel, with a catapult and crane behind it carrying an Arado Ar 196 floatplane (burned out after the battle). An ensign mast stands above the after rangefinder. In December 1939 she wore pattern camouflage, darker irregular stripes on superstructure and turrets, and a white false bow wave (the 'moustache') painted on both bows. The ship's badge was on the bow and the eagle crest on the stern. During the merchant raids from late November she carried a dummy turret on the bridge and a dummy second funnel behind the catapult. These were removed on 12 December, so she had neither in the battle or at Montevideo. At Montevideo she showed shell holes and splinter scars on the hull and tower.

facts.fact: Deutschland-class; 186 m; six 28 cm guns in two triple turrets fore and aft; eight 15 cm guns in single mounts amidships; Arado Ar 196 on a catapult with no hangar
In late November 1939 the crew built a dummy turret on the bridge and a dummy second funnel; these were removed on 12 December

Montevideo photos show pattern camouflage, a false bow wave called 'The Moustache', the ship's badge forward of the hawse pipes, the burned-out Arado on the catapult, and the ensign above the after rangefinder
Ships sunk: Clement, Ashlea, Newton Beech, Huntsman, Trevanion, Africa Shell, Doric Star, Tairoa, Streonshalh
Scuttled at 20:55 on 17 December with about 40 men aboard; about 20,000 people watched

photos.shows: Graf Spee anchored off Montevideo in mid-December 1939, in camouflage (US NHHC NH 59658)
Graf Spee in Montevideo harbour after the battle, December 1939
Starboard bow at Montevideo showing the painted false bow wave ('moustache')

entities.name: Seetakt radar (FMG 39 G(gO), later FuMO 22) on Admiral Graf Spee
entities.look: A flat rectangular 'mattress' antenna grid, roughly 0.8 m x 1.8 m according to navweaps, mounted on a radar hut on top of the foretop optical rangefinder. It sits at the very top of the forward tower superstructure, directly above the main battery rangefinder. It is clearly visible in photos taken at Montevideo.

facts.fact: An FMG G(gO) 'Seetakt' set was mounted on the foretop rangefinder, described as the first radar on a German warship
A radar hut on the rangefinder tower held the prototype FMG 39 (gO) with a 0.8 m x 1.8 m mattress antenna, fitted in 1939; it was kept very secret
NHHC photo NH 59662 shows the Seetakt antenna on the main battery gun director off Montevideo

photos.shows: Close-up of the starboard forward superstructure: rangefinder with Seetakt antenna, camouflage, 15 cm guns
Port forward superstructure: shell hole, Seetakt antenna, foremast

entities.name: Scuttling of Admiral Graf Spee, River Plate estuary off Montevideo, 17 December 1939
entities.look: Evening, about 20:55. The ship lies just outside Montevideo harbour, and charges blow her apart in huge explosions and a towering pillar of smoke. The wreck settles in shallow water with the tower superstructure and turrets still above the surface, burning for days. Crowds of about 20,000 watch from shore. The German merchant ship Tacoma took off most of the crew, who were moved to the Argentine tugs Gigante and Coloso and the barge Chata Chiriguana and landed at Buenos Aires on 18 December.

facts.fact: Scuttling ordered at 20:55 on 17 December; about 20,000 watched; an Argentine tug took off the crew
Crew arrived at Buenos Aires on 18 December 1939 on the tugs Gigante and Coloso and the Chata Chiriguana

entities.name: HMS Exeter (68)
entities.look: A York-class heavy cruiser, 575 ft long. She has three twin 8-inch turrets: A and B forward, Y aft. Her two funnels are straight, unlike York's raked funnels, and set well back from a low, enclosed, streamlined bridge. She has pole masts and two fixed catapults angled in a V amidships, with a crane to starboard. After the battle she has B turret wrecked, A knocked out, a 7-degree list and a shattered bridge area.

facts.fact: York-class; straight funnels; lower streamlined bridge; three twin 8-inch turrets (A, B, Y); pole masts; two V-angled catapults
Hit seven times by 28 cm shells, with 61 killed; B turret then A knocked out; Captain F. S. Bell wounded in the face

entities.name: HMS Ajax (22)
entities.look: A Leander-class light cruiser, 554 ft 6 in long, shown as built (before her 1940 refit added a tripod mast). She carries eight 6-inch guns in four twin turrets (A and B forward, X and Y aft) and a single large funnel. She carried a Fairey Seafox floatplane on a catapult. She was Harwood's flagship. In the battle, X and Y turrets were knocked out and her mast was shot away.

facts.fact: Leander-class, pennant 22; eight 6-inch guns in four twin mountings; one Fairey Seafox; tripod mast added in 1940 refit
Harwood's flagship, commanded by Captain Charles Woodhouse; shell damage disabled turrets and destroyed her mast
Illustrated London News, 23 December 1939, shows the ship as built

photos.shows: HMS Ajax as built (Illustrated London News, 23 Dec 1939)
HMS Ajax at sea, c.1940 (Australian War Memorial P03626.016); check whether it is before or after the refit
HMS Ajax, dated 1939–45 (check it has no tripod mast before use)

entities.name: HMS Achilles (70), New Zealand Division
entities.look: A Leander-class light cruiser, the same as Ajax: eight 6-inch guns in four twin turrets and a single funnel. She flew the Royal Navy White Ensign, being HMS rather than HMNZS until 1941. Her crew was a mix of British and New Zealand sailors.

facts.fact: Leander-class; eight 6-inch guns in twin turrets; pennant 70; mixed British and New Zealand crew; 4 killed and Captain W. E. Parry wounded at the River Plate

entities.name: Henry Harwood
entities.look: A 51-year-old Royal Navy officer (born 19 January 1888), a Commodore during the battle. He wears Royal Navy officer's uniform. Just after the battle he was promoted Rear Admiral and knighted, and the IWM caption of his Montevideo arrival already calls him 'Rear Admiral Sir Henry Harwood'. I found no written description of his face or build, so match the real photos. Note that one source warns the Montevideo IWM photo has been published mirror-reversed.

facts.fact: Born 19 January 1888; appointed commodore September 1936; promoted rear admiral and knighted after the River Plate
Commanded Force G with Ajax as flagship; planned the two-pronged attack
IWM photo shows Harwood welcomed at Montevideo by British Minister Eugen Millington-Drake after arriving in Ajax

entities.name: Patrick G. G. Dove
entities.look: A British merchant captain aged about 43 (born 1896, London), master of the Shell coastal tanker Africa Shell. He was held prisoner aboard Graf Spee and became friendly with Langsdorff. He appears as himself in the 1940 film For Freedom, so stills from that film show his real face only months after the events.

facts.fact: Born 1896 in London; master of MV Africa Shell; captured 15 November 1939 in the Mozambique Channel; became friendly with Langsdorff; wrote 'I Was Graf Spee's Prisoner' (1940)
Photographed in the 1940 film For Freedom and with other ex-prisoners in Fan Fare magazine

photos.shows: Captain Dove in the 1940 film For Freedom
Dove with other former Graf Spee prisoners (Tairoa and Ashlea officers, Captain Pottinger)

entities.name: British merchant victims (Clement, Africa Shell, Doric Star, Tairoa, etc.)
entities.look: 1930s British merchant ships flying the Red Ensign: tramp steamers, cargo liners and one small coastal tanker. Graf Spee photos show them being stopped, boarded by her launch, shelled or blown up with charges, then sinking. Note that Africa Shell was a tanker, not a cargo ship.

facts.fact: Nine British merchant ships of over 50,000 tons sunk without loss of life
Clement was shelled and sunk on 30 September 1939; a photo shows her master, Captain F. C. P. Harris, standing with German officers watching
Africa Shell was a coastal tanker; Graf Spee's launch visited her and charges blew two holes in her stern

photos.shows: Clement seen from Graf Spee, 30 September 1939
Africa Shell with Graf Spee's launch alongside, 15 November 1939
Africa Shell sinking, 15 November 1939

entities.name: British merchant seamen held prisoner aboard Graf Spee
entities.look: British Merchant Navy men in civilian sea clothes, with officers and masters in merchant officers' caps and jackets. The 61 released at Montevideo were 6 captains, 9 chief engineers, 25 officers and 21 seamen, so most were officers.

facts.fact: 61 prisoners released: 6 captains, 9 chief engineers, 25 officers, 21 seamen
Merchant captains who had been prisoners laid a wreath at the 15 December Montevideo funeral of Graf Spee's dead

photos.shows: Captain Harris of Clement with German officers aboard Graf Spee, 30 September 1939
Released prisoners of war from Graf Spee in Montevideo, December 1939 (Centro de Fotografía de Montevideo)

entities.name: Crew of Admiral Graf Spee
entities.look: Kriegsmarine sailors in dark blue or white jumpers with a square collar edged with three stripes. They wear the round sailor's cap with a ribbon reading 'Kriegsmarine'.

facts.fact: Enlisted cap tally read 'Kriegsmarine'; white jumper in summer dress; collars edged with three stripes

photos.shows: Graf Spee crewmen on the north quay, Buenos Aires, 18 December 1939

entities.name: HMS Ark Royal (91) and HMS Renown (the fake fleet)
entities.look: Ark Royal is a new aircraft carrier (completed 1938) with a long flat flight deck and an island on the starboard side, carrying Fairey Swordfish biplanes. Renown is a battlecruiser in her 1939 rebuilt form. Both were in fact about 2,500 nautical miles away.

facts.fact: British signals suggested a force including Ark Royal and Renown was gathering; only Cumberland had arrived
Ark Royal and Renown were about 2,500 nautical miles away

entities.name: Hotel de Inmigrantes, Buenos Aires, and Langsdorff's funeral
entities.look: The Hotel de Inmigrantes at the port of Buenos Aires (Retiro), December 1939: a large, plain, multi-storey immigrants' hostel with long, regular rows of identical windows and a flat, unadorned facade. The building and its grounds only, with no people anywhere in the scene. The open grounds in front lie empty and quiet. These are the grounds where the interned crew were held and where Langsdorff said farewell to his men, and the building is where he died in his room. Port surroundings are visible at the edges: dock sheds, cranes, the waterfront. Overcast, sombre light, documentary photographic style of the period. The building still stands today as a museum, but show it as it looked in 1939. (Context, not shown: his funeral on 21 December went to La Chacarita cemetery with full honours, and British officers attended.)

facts.fact: Langsdorff died in his room at the Hotel de Inmigrantes; buried at La Chacarita on 21 December with full honours
British officers attended his funeral

photos.shows: Langsdorff's funeral procession, Buenos Aires, 21 December 1939 (NH 85636)

history.text: A large plain multi-storey immigrants' hostel at the port of Buenos Aires (Retiro). It still stands and is now a museum. The crew were held in its grounds, where Langsdorff said farewell to his men. His funeral on 21 December went to La Chacarita cemetery with full honours.

entities.name: Imperial German naval ensign (Langsdorff's death flag)
entities.look: The 1903–1919 Imperial war ensign: white with a black Nordic cross, a black eagle in a central roundel, and a black-white-red canton bearing an Iron Cross. It is not the 1938 swastika ensign that flew from Graf Spee.

facts.fact: Dudley Pope identifies the flag he lay on as an Imperial naval ensign

entities.name: Langsdorff's pistol
entities.look: A Mauser pistol. The photo is a modern (2017) museum photo of the weapon described as the one he used.

facts.fact: Described as the Mauser pistol Langsdorff used to take his own life

shots.words: A German captain sank nine British cargo ships
shots.prompt: Early December 1939, South Atlantic, bright mid-morning sun on a calm deep-blue sea. Medium shot over the shoulder of Langsdorff in his white summer jacket and white-covered peaked cap, standing on the bridge wing of Admiral Graf Spee, binoculars lowered. Past him the bow with its painted white false bow wave and camouflage stripes. Ahead on the horizon a stopped 1930s British tramp steamer flies the Red Ensign. Raider-period disguise is visible: a dummy turret on the bridge and a dummy second funnel behind the catapult. Slow push-in toward the merchant ship.

shots.words: without killing a single person,
shots.prompt: Midday, harsh overhead sun. Wide shot at sea level: the British cargo ship is blown up by German scuttling charges amidships, settling by the stern in a burst of spray and smoke. In the foreground two full lifeboats of British merchant seamen in civilian sea clothes row safely clear, every man accounted for. A Graf Spee launch with Kriegsmarine sailors in white jumpers and Kriegsmarine cap ribbons escorts them. Static camera with a gentle sea bob.

shots.words: and whenever he took a crew prisoner,
shots.prompt: Afternoon, warm slanting light. Medium-wide shot from Graf Spee's deck at the accommodation ladder. Kriegsmarine sailors in white jumpers with square three-stripe collars help British merchant officers in caps and jackets, and a few seamen with small bundles, climb up from the launch. The camouflaged hull plating and a 15 cm gun mount fill the frame edge, and the smoke of the sunk cargo ship drifts on the horizon. Handheld feel, slight tilt up as the men reach the deck.

shots.words: he welcomed them and apologized for sinking their ship.
shots.prompt: Evening, below decks in the prisoners' quarters, warm yellow electric lamplight on grey steel bulkheads. Langsdorff in the midnight-blue Kriegsmarine service uniform (four gold sleeve rings under a gold star, cap with a single row of gold oak leaves) shakes hands with Captain Patrick Dove, a British merchant master about 43 in a merchant officer's cap and jacket. Langsdorff's head is slightly bowed in apology, and other British merchant officers look on. Close-medium two-shot with a slow dolly around them.

shots.words: But when some British warships
shots.prompt: 13 December 1939, just after dawn off the River Plate. A low golden sun sits behind a silvery sea. Wide shot from Ajax's bridge level: Commodore Harwood in Royal Navy officer's uniform raises binoculars in the foreground. Ajax's forward A and B twin 6-inch turrets train out, and her single funnel and pre-war pole mast stand behind. Astern follows her identical sister Achilles, flying the White Ensign. Both cruisers fire, with orange muzzle flashes and brown cordite smoke. Camera pans with the turrets.

shots.words: hit his ship about 70 times,
shots.prompt: Morning battle light, hazy with gun smoke. Medium-wide shot of Admiral Graf Spee at speed, now without the dummy turret or second funnel. British shells burst against her tall tower superstructure and hull, raising splinters, fire and tall white shell splashes alongside. Her two triple 28 cm turrets fire back. Far on the horizon HMS Exeter, listing, with two straight funnels and B turret smoking, flashes her remaining guns. The camera shakes slightly with each impact.

shots.words: he ended up limping into a port in Uruguay,
shots.prompt: Around midnight, 13–14 December 1939. Dark water of Montevideo harbour lit by scattered shore lights and the ship's dim deck lamps. Slow tracking shot along Admiral Graf Spee as she creeps in at low speed. Shell holes and splinter scars mark her hull and tower, the burned-out Arado floatplane sits by the catapult behind the single funnel, and a faint wisp of smoke trails off. The city skyline twinkles in the background.

shots.words: where he was told he had only 72 hours to leave,
shots.prompt: Grey overcast afternoon, 15 December, at anchor in Montevideo harbour. Medium close-up of Langsdorff, weary from his battle wounds, in midnight-blue service uniform, reading a typed official notice on the quarterdeck. Behind him the shell-scarred after turret and the Montevideo waterfront buildings. Slow push-in on his face as he lowers the paper.

shots.words: while the British sent fake radio messages
shots.prompt: Night, Graf Spee's cramped radio room, lit by amber dial lamps and a single shaded bulb. Close shot of a Kriegsmarine radio operator in a dark blue jumper with headphones, pencilling down an intercepted message in Morse as receiver needles flicker. Another sailor leans in to read it. Shallow focus moving from his hand to the paper.

shots.words: that a huge fleet with an aircraft carrier
shots.prompt: Dreamlike rumoured image, pale washed-out haze, styled as imagined rather than real: the faded, semi-transparent silhouettes of the carrier Ark Royal, with long flat flight deck, starboard island and Swordfish biplanes ranged on deck, and the 1939 rebuilt battlecruiser Renown, steaming in line through sea mist. Low-angle wide shot with a slow drift forward. The vision flickers like a radio signal.

shots.words: was waiting outside to seize his ship
shots.prompt: Dusk, 16 December. Purple-orange sky over the wide brown River Plate estuary. From high on Graf Spee's tower, over Langsdorff's shoulder as he scans with binoculars: the river mouth is almost empty, with only two faint cruiser silhouettes, Ajax and Achilles, single funnels, patrolling far out in the haze. Static frame, very slow zoom toward the horizon.

shots.words: but since it carried Germany's secret new radar
shots.prompt: Early morning, 17 December, clean cool light from a low sun. Low-angle close-up looking up the forward tower superstructure of Admiral Graf Spee to the main rangefinder. On top of it the radar hut carries the flat rectangular Seetakt 'mattress' antenna grid, about 0.8 by 1.8 m, against a pale blue sky. Splinter scars show on the tower plating. Slow tilt up to the antenna.

shots.words: there was no way he would let them take it,
shots.prompt: Midday, 17 December, bright flat light. Medium shot of Langsdorff in midnight-blue service uniform and gold-oak-leaf cap on the forward deck, looking up at the tower and its radar antenna, jaw set, hands clasped behind his back. The forward triple 28 cm turret is behind him. Slow arc around him ending on his determined profile.

shots.words: So instead of giving up his country’s secrets
shots.prompt: Afternoon, 17 December, hard sun through a hatch into the radar hut and instrument spaces. Kriegsmarine sailors in dark blue jumpers smash radar and fire-control equipment with sledgehammers and feed confidential papers and code books into a fire in a steel bucket. Sparks and glass fly. Quick handheld close shots.

shots.words: he detonated explosives he had planted on board,
shots.prompt: Sunset, 17 December, just outside Montevideo harbour. The sky is deep gold to rose over the flat estuary. Langsdorff sits in a small launch pulling away with the last of the scuttling party of Kriegsmarine sailors, looking back. Behind them Admiral Graf Spee lies stopped and silent, silhouetted, her tower and turrets dark against the glow, with the charges set. Wide shot from water level, tracking with the launch.

shots.words: which tore the ship apart,
shots.prompt: 20:55, 17 December, last twilight with a deep blue sky. The scuttling charges blow Admiral Graf Spee apart: huge orange explosions burst from inside the hull and a towering pillar of black smoke rises over the River Plate. Far in the foreground on the Montevideo shore, the silhouettes of the watching crowd. Locked-off wide shot with the fireball reflected on the water.

shots.words: And since he couldn't bear anyone thinking
shots.prompt: Daytime, 19 December, Buenos Aires. Warm, slightly hazy afternoon sun. Wide shot in the grounds of the large plain multi-storey Hotel de Inmigrantes: Langsdorff in midnight-blue uniform stands before his assembled crew in dark blue and white jumpers and Kriegsmarine caps, giving his farewell. Slow push-in from behind the ranks of sailors toward him.

shots.words: he sank his ship to save his own life,
shots.prompt: Night, 19 December, a bare room in Buenos Aires. Langsdorff sits alone at a small desk writing a letter by the light of a single lamp, his face half in shadow and his cap on the desk beside him. He wears full dress uniform. Close-medium shot, very slow push-in on his pen and the page.

shots.words: three days later he shot himself .
shots.prompt: Early morning, 20 December, pale grey-blue dawn light through a window. Restrained, no body and no blood shown. Overhead shot of the Imperial German naval ensign (white with black Nordic cross, eagle roundel, black-white-red canton with Iron Cross) spread on the floor. On it rest a Mauser pistol and Langsdorff's peaked cap with its single row of gold oak leaves. Utter stillness. Slow fade to black.

1Zgi5YYJSGE_vGbqXGDGV2GbPnldjvVtXOW3TCPh.title: The Bat Bombs
lines: The American military glued tiny firebombs to live bats.
You see, during World War 2 a dentist wanted to burn down Japan's cities,
but he had no way to get fire inside them,
until he thought of bats carrying a firebomb into someone's home,
so he wrote to the White House with his idea,
where even the President agreed it was worth looking into,
but while the military prepared a test on 6000 bats, things took a bad turn where the bats escaped , and flew off with their bombs already activated,
Reaching the control tower and fuel tanks inside the military base and finally exploding, destroying the whole american base and setting the airfield on fire.

entities.name: Dr. Lytle Schuyler Adams
entities.look: An American dental surgeon from Irwin, Pennsylvania, aged about 60 in Dec 1941 to 62 in May 1943 (dates 1881–1970). He was a civilian, not in uniform. In the best-known photo he wears a bow tie and examines a bat. He was also a known inventor of an air-mail pick-up system. I could not read his face, hair or build from a source in words, so copy them from photos 1 and 2.

facts.fact: Dental surgeon and part-time inventor from Irwin, Pennsylvania
Described as a 60-year-old dentist from Irwin, PA at the time of Pearl Harbor (Journal of the History of Dentistry, 2004)
Visited Carlsbad Caverns on a New Mexico vacation and heard about Pearl Harbor on his car radio on 7 Dec 1941
Sent his proposal to the White House on 12 January 1942
Letter called the bat the 'lowest form of animal life' (wording differs slightly between sources)
Set up his lab and office in an auxiliary hangar at the Carlsbad airfield
Photo caption: wearing a bow tie while examining a bat; another shows him loading a bat bomb carrier
Was an acquaintance of First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt

photos.shows: Dr Lytle Schuyler Adams in a bow tie, examining a bat (wartime US Army photo)
'Project X-Ray leader Lytle Doc Adams loads a bat bomb carrier'
Task & Purpose composite built from US Army photos of Dr. Lytle S. Adams

entities.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
entities.look: US President, aged 59 and turning 60 on 30 Jan 1942, the month the letter arrived. He was paralysed from the waist down after his 1921 illness, wore iron leg braces, and was never shown in his wheelchair in public. Show him seated, for example at his desk. He wore civilian suits. Copy his face from the NARA wartime portrait and the photo of him signing on 8 Dec 1941.

facts.fact: Born 30 January 1882
Paralysed from the waist down after his 1921 polio diagnosis; walked short distances with iron braces; careful never to be seen using his wheelchair in public
Received Adams' letter in January 1942, passed it to William J. Donovan, and approved the plan
Widely quoted reply: 'This man is not a nut... it sounds like a perfectly wild idea but is worth looking into' (secondary sources only)

photos.shows: FDR signing the declaration of war on Japan, 8 Dec 1941, about a month before the letter (Abbie Rowe, NARA 520053)
Wartime portrait of FDR, Office of War Information, dated 1942–45 (NARA 535943)

entities.name: The White House, Washington D.C. (1942)
entities.look: White neoclassical mansion. In 1942 the curved South Portico had NO second-floor balcony, because the Truman Balcony was only finished in March 1948. Fabric awnings hung behind the columns instead. Do not use modern photos that show the balcony.

facts.fact: The Truman Balcony was finished in March 1948; before that, awnings shaded the portico
The photo of FDR's fourth inaugural (1945) shows the south face before the balcony, with awnings

photos.shows: South Portico in January 1945, with no balcony and awnings visible (FDR's 4th inaugural)

entities.name: Mexican free-tailed bats (Tadarida brasiliensis)
entities.look: A small bat about 9 cm long, weighing about 7–12 g, with dark brown to grey fur. It has wide, rounded ears that nearly meet over the face, deep wrinkles on the upper lip, and long, narrow, pointed wings. Its tail sticks out past the wing membrane. The test bats were caught at Carlsbad Caverns and chilled into hibernation before use.

facts.fact: Size, weight, colour, ears, lip wrinkles, wings and free tail
Picked because it was numerous, could carry a load, and was tough enough to survive the drop
Army officers collected the test bats from Carlsbad Caverns
Chilled to about 40°F in ice-cube trays to put them into hibernation
About 6,000 bats were used across the Army experiments (the script's '6000'). Around 3,500 were collected for the May 1943 Muroc/Carlsbad drops

photos.shows: Bats flying out of Carlsbad Caverns, NM, the source colony (modern photo)

entities.name: Napalm bat incendiary (Fieser H-2 unit)
entities.look: A tiny oblong capsule with a celluloid or nitrocellulose case, about 3/4 inch wide and 2.5 inches long, filled with napalm (thickened kerosene) gel. It hung under the bat's chest, fixed to the loose chest skin with a surgical clip and a string; some sources say it was glued. It came in two sizes, 17 g and 28 g. The 17 g unit burned about 4 minutes with a 10-inch flame. It burns rather than explodes.

facts.fact: Celluloid case about 3/4 in by 2.5 in, napalm gel, attached by surgical clip and string
17 g and 28 g sizes; 17 g burned about 4 min with a 10 in flame; delay igniter where copper chloride ate through a steel wire to release a firing pin

entities.name: Bat bomb carrier canister
entities.look: A bomb-shaped sheet-metal casing about 1.5 m (5 ft) long. Inside were 26 stacked round cardboard trays, each about 76 cm (30 in) across with 40 compartments, holding 1,040 sleeping bats in all. It was dropped by parachute, and its sides fell away at about 1,000–4,000 ft to release the bats.

entities.name: Carlsbad Army Airfield Auxiliary Air Base (Aux #1, Harkey Crossing), near Carlsbad, New Mexico
entities.look: Flat desert scrub. A satellite field about 5 miles from the main Carlsbad AAF bombardier school, built in 1942–43. It had four asphalt runways and newly built, plain wooden temporary buildings: a control tower, hangar(s), barracks, offices and a fuel tank. Main-base photos from 1944 show tar-paper barracks of this kind. It was a small field, not a big base.

entities.name: Carlsbad auxiliary field fire, 15 May 1943
entities.look: Burning wooden buildings and a smoke column over the desert airfield. Base staff were kept behind locked gates and watched, and no fire crews were called because the project was secret. Nobody was reported hurt. The fires were incendiary burns, not explosions.

entities.name: US Army Air Forces / Chemical Warfare Service personnel and Signal Corps photographers (unnamed), May 1943
entities.look: Young American enlisted men and officers in the summer khaki cotton service uniform: long-sleeved khaki twill shirt (convertible collar by 1942), khaki trousers, and from Feb 1942 a khaki tie. They wore a khaki garrison cap with branch-colour piping, an olive-drab M-1937 web belt with a frame buckle, and russet high-top service shoes. Rank chevrons sat midway between shoulder and elbow. Officers wore the same khakis with a khaki tie. There was no olive-drab wool in May in the New Mexico heat.

shots.words: The American military glued tiny firebombs to live bats.
shots.prompt: Flash-forward hook, May 1943, inside a plain wooden temporary building at the Carlsbad auxiliary field. Extreme close-up on a workbench: the hands of a young US Army soldier in a long-sleeved khaki twill shirt fix a small oblong celluloid napalm capsule (about 2.5 in long, 3/4 in wide) under the chest of a limp, chilled Mexican free-tailed bat. Show the bat's dark brown-grey fur, wide rounded ears, wrinkled upper lip, folded narrow wings and tail sticking past the membrane. The capsule hangs from the loose chest skin with a small surgical clip and string. Slow push-in, shallow depth of field, cool morning daylight from a side window. No flames.

shots.words: You see, during World War 2 a dentist
shots.prompt: December 1941, Irwin, Pennsylvania. Medium shot of Dr. Lytle S. Adams, about 60, a civilian in shirt and bow tie (face, hair and build copied from reference photos 1 and 2), standing beside a 1940s dental chair and instrument tray in his small surgery. He looks down at a folded newspaper about the war. Grey overcast winter afternoon light through a frosted window, muted cool tones. Static camera, eye level.

shots.words: wanted to burn down Japan's cities,
shots.prompt: Pre-war 1930s Tokyo residential district seen in a high wide shot: dense rows of low one- and two-storey wooden houses and shops with grey tiled roofs, narrow lanes, no modern buildings. Hazy, flat daylight, period documentary feel. Slow lateral drift across the rooftops. No fire, no aircraft; this is the target as Adams pictured it.

shots.words: but he had no way to get fire inside them,
shots.prompt: Dusk in a narrow 1930s Tokyo lane. Closer, street-level shot of one wooden two-storey house: tiled roof with deep eaves, wooden walls, sliding paper-and-wood screens shut, a paper lantern glowing by the door. Camera tilts up slowly to the dark gap under the eaves, the way into the house. Blue-hour light with a warm glow behind the paper screens. No people in focus, no flames.

shots.words: until he thought of bats carrying a firebomb into someone's home,
shots.prompt: Night, winter 1941–42, Adams's home study. Medium close-up of Dr. Adams in bow tie (face from reference photos) seated at a lamplit desk, closely examining a small Mexican free-tailed bat held in his fingers, as in his best-known photo. On the desk lies a rough pencil sketch of a bat with a small capsule under its chest beside a house roof. Warm single desk-lamp light, deep shadows, slow push-in on his face.

shots.words: so he wrote to the White House with his idea,
shots.prompt: January 1942. Wide exterior of the White House South Portico on a grey winter morning: white neoclassical mansion with a curved colonnade, fabric awnings behind the columns, and NO second-floor (Truman) balcony. Bare trees, light snow on the lawn, pale overcast sky. Slow dolly-in. Period-accurate, no modern details.

shots.words: where even the President agreed it was worth looking into,
shots.prompt: January 1942, White House office interior. Medium shot of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, 59–60, in a dark civilian suit, seated behind his desk (no wheelchair or leg braces visible; face copied from the NARA wartime portrait and the 8 Dec 1941 signing photo). He reads a typed letter, nods, and writes a short note on it with a fountain pen. Warm afternoon lamplight mixed with soft window light, flags and desk items behind him. Gentle static framing.

shots.words: but while the military prepared a test on 6000 bats,
shots.prompt: 15 May 1943, Carlsbad Army Airfield auxiliary field (Harkey Crossing), New Mexico. Wide establishing shot on a clear, bright desert morning: flat scrub, asphalt runway, a few plain new wooden temporary buildings including a small control tower and a hangar, an olive-drab B-25C/D Mitchell with a glazed nose and twin tails parked nearby. Young soldiers in summer khaki shirts, trousers, ties and garrison caps carry stacked round cardboard trays of chilled, sleeping bats toward a 5-ft sheet-metal bomb-shaped canister. Crisp morning sun, long soft shadows. A small field, not a big base.

shots.words: things took a bad turn
shots.prompt: Midday, same field. Close-up from above on an open cardboard tray compartment sitting in harsh overhead sun: chilled Mexican free-tailed bats, each with a small celluloid napalm capsule clipped under its chest, begin to warm and stir. One bat twitches its narrow wings and lifts its head. A soldier's khaki sleeve is just in frame. Hard white noon light, heat shimmer, tense slow zoom.

shots.words: where the bats escaped ,
shots.prompt: Midday. Low-angle shot from tray level as several bats flutter up and away past a startled young soldier in khaki shirt and garrison cap, his hands reaching too late. Capsules visible under the bats' chests. Bright blue sky, harsh sun, quick tilt up following the bats.

shots.words: and flew off with their bombs already activated,
shots.prompt: Early afternoon. Long-lens shot of a few small bats flying low over desert scrub toward the auxiliary field's wooden buildings, each with a small oblong capsule hanging under its chest (unlit, timed igniters armed). Heat haze, bright but slightly warmer afternoon light. Camera tracks the bats from behind.

shots.words: Reaching the control tower and fuel tanks
shots.prompt: Afternoon. Two-part composition in one frame: in the foreground, bats with capsules clinging and crawling into the shaded eaves of the plain wooden control tower; in the background, bats settling near the base of the field's fuel tank. Raw new timber and tar paper, warm afternoon side light, deep shade under the eaves. Slow pan from tower to tank.

shots.words: inside the military base and finally exploding,
shots.prompt: Late afternoon. Close-up under the eaves of a wooden building: a napalm capsule ignites with a sudden burst of bright orange flame about 10 inches tall that licks up the dry wooden boards (an incendiary flare-up, not a blast; no shockwave or debris). Flickering firelight against warm low sun. Quick punch-in on the flame.

shots.words: destroying the whole american base
shots.prompt: Late afternoon, golden light. Wide shot of the small auxiliary field: the wooden control tower and a hangar engulfed in flames, fire spreading through wooden buildings, a thick black smoke column rising over the desert. No explosions and no fire trucks. Slow crane-up revealing the burning buildings across the flat field.

shots.words: and setting the airfield on fire.
shots.prompt: Sunset. Extreme wide shot from behind a locked wire gate: silhouetted base staff in khaki uniforms and garrison caps stand and watch, unable to act, as the smoke column and orange glow rise over the asphalt runways and burning wooden buildings across the desert. No fire crews. Deep orange and red sky, long shadows, slow pull-back to end.
